Defending the nationwide student protests over the paper leak as a peaceful expression of youthful aspiration, he recounted a conversation with an eighteen-year-old who’d sorted people into three categories: students, idiots, and andhbhakts who follow the idiots. The side of parliament where ruling party MPs and ministers sit erupted. One of the ministers rose to demand that the word “idiot” be struck from the record as unparliamentary. Speaker Om Birla had to intervene repeatedly just to restore order.

The two instances, to outsiders and those in the ruling benches, may appear lacking in discipline. But this is what a parliamentary system actually looks like — those in the ruling segment can’t ignore the people arguing with it.

Go further out West and this model gets sharper. In the UK, British Prime Minister’s Questions is a much mocked ritual, one that has now outlasted seven different prime ministers just in the past decade. The thirty minutes of unscripted, grandiose session produces more heat than information. But beneath the mockery is a format that forces accountability. In April, Commons Speaker Lindsay Hoyle stopped Prime Minister Keir Starmer mid-session and told him plainly that it was Prime Minister’s Questions, not a chance to attack the opposition leader instead of answering. The rebuke was serious enough that Starmer, who left office earlier this month, confronted him about it afterward. Hoyle’s office was unapologetic, telling reporters that reminding a prime minister of the rules of engagement is simply part of the job, and that this wasn’t a one-off.

There’s a common thread in both examples: the Speaker’s party doesn’t decide which way he leans once he’s in the chair. Om Birla is a ruling Bharatiya Janata Party MP, but he has to rule on the minister’s objection. Lindsay Hoyle came up through Parliament as a Labour MP, and he still pulled up a Labour prime minister for dodging questions. In a parliamentary system, that chair asks something drastically different of the person than the party did.

Nepal’s Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal walked into the chair straight from being the Rastriya Swatantra Party’s vice-chair, elected unopposed because his party holds a near two-thirds majority in the House. Opposition lawmakers have spent months accusing him of failing to compel Shah’s appearance and of leaning toward the government. On Thursday, he faced a test: lawmaker after lawmaker rose demanding the government answer for the communal violence in Sunsari district and the prime minister’s absence from it, and Aryal had the authority to rule that the House was owed a response. He failed.

This brings us to the elephant in the room, the prime minister himself. Balendra Shah has faced the parliament exactly once, on May 31, and it looked nothing like the Question Hour. It was his first session answering lawmakers. He was asked about the old border dispute with India, he said Nepal had also encroached on Indian land in places — a fact, he said, he’d only learned after taking office — and suggested the UK be brought in to help resolve it alongside India. You’d think a government would spend days, even weeks, preparing a statement like that before saying it on the record. Shah delivered it like an aside.

The backlash was immediate. The Nepali Congress and CPN-UML demanded he retract the statement, produce evidence, and apologize. Former Nepali ambassadors to India said publicly that no such encroachment had ever been documented. Opposition lawmakers picketed the well of the House and called for his resignation. Shah did not come back to answer follow-up questions. When his own party’s chief whip was asked why, the answer was the government’s own defense: parliamentary rules don’t require the prime minister’s personal presence, and a minister can respond on his behalf.

When Shah did resurface again, this time on June 1, it wasn’t to answer for the substance. He arrived unannounced, addressed the House briefly through the Speaker, and repeated the claim rather than walk it back. Opposition Chief Whip Ain Bahadur Mahar’s complaint that day said as much about the moment as the remark itself: he objected not only to what Shah had said, but to what he’d worn as he said it, arguing the prime minister was dressed for the football pitch rather than Parliament. Two months later, Shah still hasn’t addressed the House on the matter again.

This week, the pattern became impossible to ignore. As communal unrest that started on Sunday spread across towns in the southern plains, the death toll rose to three. Shah skipped the all-party meeting his own coalition partner convened to address the situation, and he addressed the killings only through a Facebook post. Speaker Aryal met with Shah on Tuesday and told him “it would be good” if he kept the House informed about the country’s current situation. Shah’s response? “I’ll think about it.”

When the Parliament finally reconvened on Thursday after a 15-day recess, it gave the crisis unfolding in the southern plains a special hour. Shah, once again, was nowhere to be seen. Most of the lawmakers who spoke, including former prime minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal, used their time to ask where Shah was; Dahal pointedly noted that the prime minister and his home minister had also skipped the all-party meeting. Aryal had the chance to rule that the government owed the House an answer, but he said nothing. Instead of forcing one, he adjourned the session again — this time for five days. Hours later, Shah addressed the nation for the first time since taking office, in a pre-recorded video that was posted on his personal Facebook page.

Nepal has all the same paper machinery as Delhi or London. It has a chapter of procedure devoted to questioning the prime minister directly. Even KP Sharma Oli — a prime minister widely criticized for his governing style — kept showing up to take questions from the opposition, session after session. He’d occasionally refuse to answer one he didn’t like, calling it hostile, but he came back the next time anyway.

Balendra Shah has refused to come back at all.

articles.title: Bhanubhakta beyond Ramayan: The other side of Nepal’s most revered poet
articles.summary:
This year’s Bhanu Jayanti came and went, as it does every year, without much controversy. The day saw celebratory poem-recitation competitions, extended morning assemblies in schools, and the general commemorations expected on the day.

Students, teachers and public figures alike spoke about Bhanubhakta’s translation of the Ramayan into Nepali and his general contributions to the language.

But 'Badhu Siksha’, Acharya’s prescriptive poem for the education of women, did not receive broad attention. In one stanza of the poem, Acharya instructs women to follow a life of devotion and service to their husbands, whom he says are no less than the gods. In another part, he warns that a woman who laughs risks becoming a beshya, a prostitute, and if not that, then risks at the least letting her house fall into disarray.

Ram Chandra Paudel, an associate professor of Nepali language and literature, who has been teaching for 25 years in Kathmandu University, shared that the poem was aimed at the wife and daughter-in-law of one of Bhanubhakta’s close friends, Tarapati. After witnessing the conflict-stricken state of Tarapati’s family affairs, he is said to have written the poem. Paudel also said that the poem is considered to be among Bhanubhakta’s minor works.

Bhushita Vasistha, a writer and researcher of Nepali and Sanskrit who recited Acharya’s ‘Badhu Sikshya’ with Nepalaya’s ‘Paleti’ in 2023, was the harshest in her criticism of the poem.

“I think the poem is degrading to women. The treatment of women in the poem is akin to that of livestock. Women are asked to contain their jealousy if their husband brings home another wife. There is no space for individuation and self-actualisation for women,” she said.

“Viewed from a modern feminist lens, there is definitely space to be critical of the poem. Nepal has always been a patriarchal society, one that is not critical of its men. Acharya does not comment on what his friend, Tarapati, himself could do better. If his house is in disarray, he must be part of the reason why, but he is not told what to do,” said Shiva Gopal Risal, an eminent professor of Nepali language and literature and author of 115 books. He was affiliated, for most of his career, with Padma Kanya Campus. Risal was among the first cohort of students to study Nepali at Tribhuvan University when it was established.

“Bhanu Bhakta’s poem is an example of the sort of education that women were given in his time. In particular, it is aimed at daughters-in-law. The prescriptions in the poem align with what many women's lives were like at the time. Even today, women might face similar expectations. Women at the time were, obviously, not going to school. They would get married off by their fathers into unfamiliar homes. At a time like that, when daughter-in-laws would have been beholden to their families, it was the only way to get by,” he added.

None of the experts were in favour of banning the work.

“People are not sheep. We need to have the courage to let people speak their mind. The sovereignty of the individual is the most important thing. We need to protect everybody’s freedom of speech,” Vasistha says.

“The poem is instructive. The mother-in-law is not the enemy of the daughter-in-law. She does not have to be cruel and suppressive, yet many mother-in-laws are. If the daughter-in-law does not protest, conflict is avoided. If she is of a nature where she won’t just take everything coming her way, there are problems. The poem is just as important today as it was when it was written. Ultimately, it teaches that women are not each other’s enemies, that they must learn to understand each other's problems,” Paudel said.

Experts also spoke of the value the poem carries.

“It is important because it is an archaeological history. It gives us rare insight into the society of the time. For example, the poem mentions Sati pratha; we learn then that Sati pratha was part of that society.” Additionally, Vasistha also praised the poem’s elegant use of meter.

“Like I said before, the poem is a living history in some ways. We are hearing the predominant opinion on these matters from a person of prominence and education in his time. Whatever one's views on the poem, it is important because it conveys some facts about society,” Risal said.

For example, in one part, the poem speaks of treating the members of the family to raisins, cashews and almonds. In another part, the poem speaks of how servants are to be dealt with. These lines tell readers that Tarapati would have been a rich man, that he had servants in his household and that people of his social class would have considered raisins, cashews and almonds to be special treats.

“The reason for this is the same as why Nepal’s bureaucracy has so many problems. People respect authority beyond reason. Acharya is a canonised figure in Nepal. People are not comfortable with criticising someone with the moniker of Adikavi”, Vasistha said.

Paudel shared that many of his students were unaware of who Bhanubhakta was, let alone be familiar with a minor work of his like ‘Badhu Sikshya’. Of readers who were familiar, he shared that readers were both respectful of his contributions and, in their place, critical of the poem for the same reasons that he was.

“With time, older ideas are challenged and fall out of fashion, the same thing is happening with ‘Badhu Sikshya', and it will continue to happen. This is not an extraordinary matter,” said Risal.

articles.title: A rom-com that learns to let go
articles.summary:
Eventually, Sharanya Rajgopal’s ‘Musafir Cafe’ settles into the cosiness of a novel found in a railway station bookstall. Those unintimidating 200-page paperbacks, which one buys for an overnight journey. Here, it happens in the seventh episode of this eight-episode series. Sudha (Vedika Pinto) is a pretty, impulsive, recklessly-ambitious girl from Bhopal – a version of a metropolitan idea of a small-town firebrand. The kind who discovered ‘Carpe Diem’ in her adolescence and never looked back. She has a job offer from Mumbai, which she reluctantly accepts.

Unfortunately, she’s in love with Chander (Vikrant Massey), who she met a few months ago, and is currently vacationing with, in Mussoorie. Chander, a US-returned engineer who harbours dreams of owning a cafe on a hill station, is the opposite of Sudha. He’s excited about Mussoorie, his boss has agreed to become his loan guarantor, and he might have also found a business partner.

Sudha hasn’t told Chander about her plans yet. And when she does – he quashes his plans, and talks about moving with her to Mumbai. This disappoints her. In a rather pragmatic moment in the show, Sudha shames Chander for flippantly giving up on his dreams, and choosing to follow her instead. Some of her respect diminishes for him. This scene is what the entire series is building towards – and it reveals a sincere relationship drama embedded within the glossy design of a staple Netflix rom-com.

Based on Divya Prakash Dubey’s novel of the same name, Rajgopal’s series doesn’t begin with the same assurance. There’s an inherent clash between the show’s earthy source material and the frothy, urban Netflix aesthetic (that makes Bhopal look like Andheri). The actors, Pinto as Sudha and Massey as Chander, look (and sound) very protagonist-y. They’re not ‘ordinary’ by any measure.

Chander has been asked to meet with Sudha at a cafe, as an arranged-marriage prospect. Sudha is transparently cruel as he tells him marriage is not on her radar, and that she does this to please her mother. Chander, a pragmatic nerd with low self-esteem, finds himself charmed by her lack of filter. An unsuccessful arranged marriage meet-up improvises into an unintentional first date.

Directed by Ruchir Arun, who spearheaded the walk-and-talk relationship dramas on India’s Youtube (like Little Things), even ‘Musafir Cafe’ has plenty of the genre’s ‘relatable’ affectations. Massey, usually an effortless actor, initially looks at sea with the narrative sparseness. There’s very little to Chander beyond his desire to get married, and his infatuation with Sudha. A quirk added for effect, where he’s particular about his coffee, never feels like an innate part of him. Pinto is unconvincing as a girl from Ratlam, especially with that body language that belongs in Soho House.

The humour, and the abrupt relationship expediency, feel contrived at first.

Things become more easy-going in the third and fourth episode

However, things become more easy-going in the third and fourth episode, when Chander’s mother (Anubha Fatehpuria), shows up unannounced. A scene featuring Sudha’s roommate, a staple scene in such shows, when the two girls giggle over Sudha’s brand-new partner, is cute.

Even though they’re hopelessly in love, they’re both aware it could be a fleeting thing. He wants to settle down in the hills, she wants to go to Mumbai and afford a life many only dream about. They’ve fundamentally opposite goals in life, something one will invariably have to ‘adjust’ for.

The more mature track unfolds in the present, (Chander & Sudha’s love story is shown to have taken place eight years before), where Chander has realised his dream of Musafir Cafe, in Mussoorie. It’s run by him and his partner, Preeti (Manisha Makhwana). It looks 3-D printed out of Instagram, given how there’s not a single smudge on the cafe’s table cloths.

The surprising detail here is that Preeti knows about Chander’s lack-of-closure with Sudha. She’s the generous lover, who rationalises her partner’s flaws on his behalf, and doesn’t allow any form of negativity. It’s an interesting relationship dynamic, where a woman patiently waits for her man to leave behind his past.

Preeti is so close to an ideal, and so plainly characterised, I’m tempted to call her an invention of the male gaze. Which is not to say, she’s not disarming. Makhwana plays the stoic Preeti using a light touch, who would rather silently suffer for her lover, than show signs of jealousy. When Sudha visits them in Mussoorie late in the show, she puts up a brave front as a host, and then weeps at home.

Like Preeti’s sadness here, the show fetishises some other things too. A writer character (Rajeev Siddhartha), who talks like he’s writing prose. Always dressed immaculately in dark overcoats, sipping tea/coffee as young girls (his fans) giggle around him, he doesn’t miss a beat flirting with Preeti (an aspiring writer, we’re told).

Also, the dream of owning a cafe in the hills feels like a very city-bred fantasy. There’s nothing to indicate that Chander and Preeti are struggling at all, as the cafe appears to be running itself. People come in, and speak in Instagram affirmations. ‘Musafir’ assumes an Imtiaz Ali metaphor for many, who look forward to the journey, rather than the destination. Most of them appear to be in search of themselves.

It could seem laughable from a distance, but I found myself smitten by the fantasy. It’s the kind of show where a business partner signs away his palatial chalet to Chander and Preeti before moving back to the US for good – which they can use for expansion.

After trudging along cliches of the will they/won’t they rom-com, ‘Musafir Cafe’ becomes the strongest version of itself in the final two episodes, when an older couple enters the picture. Played by Adil Hussain and Sadiya Siddiqui, they become the (high) benchmark for Chander.

As Sudha visits Chander one last time, before moving abroad for good, they have an awkward at first, but ultimately cathartic conversation, bringing closure to both of them. It’s a rare sight of exes being shown as both graceful and grateful around each other. If not for the relationship, they wouldn’t be the people they are today. Each failed relationship is also a coming-of-age tale. That’s a realisation few relationship dramas seem to have.

Arun and Rajgopal take a good call of ending things on a crescendo of ambiguity, rather than a neatly-tied climax with a slate of ‘The End’. It mimics the beats of a life that goes on long after the ‘story’ has concluded. I’d love for them to just leave it at that, instead of using the open end for a season two. Sometimes closure isn’t about certainty, it’s about knowing when to let go. Let’s hope Netflix does too.

articles.title: Book review: When folklore becomes fear
articles.summary:
Nepali horror has often found itself caught between two impulses: imitating familiar western supernatural fiction or leaning so heavily on folklore that it becomes little more than a catalogue of ghosts and legends. ‘Aghortantra’ attempts something more ambitious.

It borrows from oral traditions, Tantric mysticism, village myths and psychological suspense to create a horror novel that feels unmistakably rooted in Nepal. While the novel occasionally loses momentum under the weight of its own mythology, it succeeds in proving that local landscapes and belief systems can be just as unsettling as any haunted castle or Gothic mansion.

The novel follows an unnamed narrator struggling with fragmented memories and recurring nightmares. Accompanying his friend Muskan to a remote village in Rukum, he expects little more than a visit to the countryside. Instead, he stumbles into a place haunted not merely by spirits but by its own forgotten history. Strange dreams, abandoned caves, unexplained disappearances and stories passed down through generations slowly reveal a web of ancient rituals and curses that binds the village to forces far older than its inhabitants.

What makes ‘Aghortantra’ compelling is that it never rushes towards its monsters. The novel understands that fear grows best through anticipation.

Long before anything overtly supernatural appears, the landscape itself begins to feel hostile. Forests seem to remember forgotten tragedies. Rivers separate more than villages. Caves cease to be geological formations and become living repositories of secrets. Animals react to unseen presences before humans do. By allowing atmosphere to carry much of the horror, the novel recalls the rhythms of oral ghost stories told in Nepali villages, where silence and suggestion often prove more frightening than revelation.

The book's greatest strength lies in its mythology. Rather than importing vampires, demons or other well-worn horror figures, it builds its supernatural world from local belief systems. Dhamis, ritual purification, sacred ash, village legends and Tantric practices are woven into the narrative not as exotic decoration but as living traditions that shape how the characters understand danger. The supernatural never feels detached from everyday life because, for the villagers, these beliefs are everyday life. Their understanding of the world is informed by inherited stories as much as by observable reality.

This cultural grounding gives ‘Aghortantra’ an identity that distinguishes it from much contemporary horror. Even readers familiar with the genre will find themselves navigating unfamiliar terrain. The horror emerges not simply from what lurks in the forest, but from the possibility that the stories dismissed as superstition may contain uncomfortable truths.

The novel also avoids reducing its characters to victims waiting for supernatural punishment. The friendship between the narrator and Muskan provides the emotional centre of the story. Their bond develops naturally through shared danger rather than melodramatic declarations, lending emotional weight to the increasingly bizarre events around them. Muskan, in particular, acts as the novel's moral compass: brave without being reckless, compassionate without becoming sentimental. Their relationship keeps the narrative grounded when the mythology threatens to become overwhelming.

Equally effective is the way the novel treats memory. The narrator's forgotten past mirrors the village's suppressed history. As buried legends resurface, so do fragments of his own identity. This parallel transforms the novel from a simple ghost story into something more reflective. The real horror is not merely that evil exists, but that communities and individuals alike cannot escape what they choose to forget. Ancient mistakes continue to shape the present, suggesting that the past is never truly buried.

Yet ‘Aghortantra’ is also a novel that asks for patience. Its fascination with mythology occasionally works against its storytelling. Lengthy explanations of village legends and ritual histories interrupt scenes just as they begin to gather momentum. There are moments when readers understand the implications of a legend before the narrative has finished explaining it.

Repetition, too, becomes noticeable. Characters frequently respond to danger in similar ways, and descriptions of fear sometimes echo one another closely. A firmer editorial hand could have tightened these sections without sacrificing the richness of world-building.

The supporting character, while colourful, rarely develops beyond their narrative function. Characters such as Kiran, Dorje and several villagers primarily exist to guide the protagonists through successive mysteries or supply pieces of folklore. Although this helps sustain the atmosphere, it occasionally leaves emotional investment concentrated almost entirely on the central friendship.

Perhaps the novel's boldest decision is its refusal to provide complete closure. While the immediate supernatural threat appears contained, the ending suggests that deeper mysteries remain unresolved. Instead of presenting evil as something permanently defeated, ‘Aghortantra’ portrays it as cyclical, waiting for history to repeat itself. The final pages imply that the protagonist's journey has only begun, resisting the temptation to explain every mystery. For some readers this ambiguity may prove frustrating; for others it will be precisely what lingers after the final page.

In recent years, Nepali genre fiction has steadily expanded beyond romance and social realism, and ‘Aghortantra’ demonstrates how horror can contribute meaningfully to that growth. Its greatest achievement is not that it frightens readers—though it often does—but that it trusts Nepali folklore to sustain an entire fictional universe. Rather than borrowing its fears from elsewhere, it discovers them in the country's own forests, rivers, rituals and oral traditions.

‘Aghortantra’ is an uneven novel, but it is also an imaginative and culturally confident one. It shows that horror need not abandon local identity to become compelling. By turning inherited myths into living nightmares, it opens intriguing possibilities for the future of Nepali speculative fiction.

articles.title: Budget-friendly places for Nepali students in Ohio
articles.summary:
Athens is a small, scenic college town in southeastern Ohio, shaped largely by Ohio University and its energetic student community. Surrounded by rolling hills, rivers and forests, the town combines historic streets, local businesses and easy access to nature.

The university campus, downtown shops and restaurants are concentrated within a compact area, making daily life manageable without a car. Ohio University students can also use Athens Public Transit free of charge, while nearby trails and forests provide inexpensive options for hiking and outdoor recreation.

Because Athens is a relatively small town, the number of professional internships available locally can be limited. Although Ohio University hosts career fairs and attracts employers from across the country, students may need to look beyond Athens or relocate temporarily for specialised opportunities.

Oxford is a compact, classic college town in southwestern Ohio, built almost entirely around Miami University at its core. Red-brick Georgian buildings, leafy streets and a walkable uptown give it a traditional campus-town character.

The compact layout means campus, uptown restaurants, shops and student housing are all within easy walking distance. The town is also considered quite safe, and Miami University's strong sense of community brings a steady calendar of campus events, traditions and activities that keep student life active without needing to travel elsewhere.

The town's economy is heavily tied to the university, so it can feel quiet or emptied out during breaks and summer months when students are away.

ColumbusColumbus is Ohio's capital and largest city, and it's where The Ohio State University, one of the biggest campuses in the country, is situated. Rather than a self-contained college town, Columbus functions as a full city with sprawling neighborhoods, a job market, and student population that's just one part of a much bigger urban picture.

Pros:Living costs stay reasonable even with everything a major city offers, and students get real exposure to internships and employers across finance, tech, healthcare and government without having to leave town.

Cons:The scale of the city brings more traffic and scattered housing options, so building a close community takes a bit more intention than it would in a smaller town.

Cincinnati is moving to universities like the University of Cincinnati and Xavier University. The city has 300,000 people and many residential areas.

Pros:The city offers people a diverse job market. It is home to many consumer goods, finance and healthcare companies. The cost of living is on the lower end for cities of this size.

Cons:Despite its universities, the city is not generally considered a college town. Younger residents have to actively seek college-town experiences since it is not part of city life. The city is also not walkable.

Toledo is Ohio’s fourth largest city, sitting on the edge of Lake Erie. It is a city of 600,000 people and home to the University of Toledo.

Pros: The University of Toledo sits at the centre of city life. It is the biggest school in town and also the town's biggest employer. Students have a solid pipeline to work experience and internships.

Cons: As a Rust Belt city, its growth has been stagnant over the years. And despite its size, it is considered to be falling behind the other major metros in Ohio.

Based on conversations with local Nepali students in Ohio.

articles.title: Migrant workers can strike under new Qatari labour law
articles.summary:
The Qatari government has introduced a conditional right for migrant workers to stage legal strikes as part of amendments to the country’s labour law.

Under the revised law, workers can go on strike for up to six working days after notifying their employer and the Ministry of Labour in writing, but only if a labour dispute cannot be resolved through negotiation, conciliation or mediation. The provision was introduced through Qatar’s Law No 9 of 2026, which amended the 2004 Labour Law (Law No 14) to strengthen workers’ rights and welfare.

The amended law requires companies with 100 or more employees to establish joint committees made up of management and worker representatives. The committees are intended to improve workplace dialogue, strengthen consultation and help resolve disputes before they escalate.

The reforms also introduce tougher penalties for labour violations. Employers that breach wage protection regulations may face suspension of ministry services, while the Labour Dispute Resolution Committee has been formally authorised to conduct virtual hearings. Recruitment agencies and companies involved in hiring violations may face fines ranging from QAR3,000 to QAR25,000. One Qatari riyal is equivalent to Rs41.66.

Workers exercising their right to strike will not be entitled to wages during the strike period. The law also allows companies to dismiss without notice workers who organise illegal or unjustified strikes without following the required procedures or who disrupt business operations through such actions.

Companies that fail to establish mandatory joint committees may face fines ranging from QAR2,000 to QAR5,000.

Qatar has also strengthened enforcement of its Wage Protection System. The amended law gives the labour ministry greater authority to take action against employers that delay or fail to pay salaries, including suspending services, imposing administrative measures and applying regulatory penalties against repeat offenders.

If a company repeatedly violates wage rules or triggers collective disputes because of unpaid salaries, other companies under the same ownership may also face penalties. The ministry may publish the names of non-compliant companies on its website.

Workers who remain unpaid can request a change of employer or terminate their contracts, with repatriation costs to be covered by the employer.

The Labour Dispute Resolution Committee’s new authority to conduct virtual hearings means workers no longer need to be physically present to pursue labour cases. Employers, workers and verified witnesses can now participate in proceedings online.

Workers must first register disputes with the ministry. Cases are referred to the dispute resolution committee only when efforts to settle them through negotiation fail. Agreements reached through ministry-led mediation will have the status of legally enforceable documents.

The amended law also increases penalties for recruitment-related violations.

Recruitment agencies can be fined between QAR3,000 and QAR25,000 for hiring workers without ministry approval for employment contracts, processing recruitment before mandatory medical examinations or committing other administrative and recruitment-related violations.

Qatari recruitment agencies generally recruit workers in partnership with manpower agencies in Nepal, although some employers also hire directly through Nepali firms.

The new rules also require workers seeking employment in designated technical and professional occupations to obtain certificates confirming that they have completed required training and passed examinations at ministry-approved centres before starting work.

Meanwhile, Qatar has extended the non-compete period, during which an employee can be restricted from joining a competing company after leaving a job, from one year to two years. The change restores a provision that existed before 2020.

If an employee has access to sensitive client information, trade secrets or confidential company data, an employer can prevent them from joining a competitor for up to two years after the termination of employment.

The labour law amendments are aimed at modernising Qatar’s labour market, improving regulatory oversight and creating a more flexible and competitive employment system in line with the Qatar National Vision 2030. Some provisions will require additional decrees and executive regulations before they come into full effect.

“These reforms represent significant shifts that will heavily impact employers, workers, recruitment agencies and the dispute resolution system alike,” Krishna Panthi, president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association Qatar, told Kantipur.

articles.title: 67 Nepalis died in Japan over ten months, 25 killed themselves
articles.summary:
As many as 67 Nepali citizens have died in Japan over the past ten months, including 25 suicides, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Most of the deceased were individuals who had travelled on student visas and were also working part-time.

The deaths were recorded between mid-July, 2025 and June 1, 2026. While some cases list medical or other causes, many certificates state the reason as “unknown”. Illness-related deaths remain relatively low, officials said.

Acting Nepali ambassador to Japan Harihar Kant Poudel said the rising number of deaths has made body management increasingly difficult. “In some cases, families perform the funeral rites in Japan. In others, the embassy is not informed even after cremation,” he said.

Repatriating a body from Japan to Nepal costs around Rs1.2 million. Educational institutions sending students abroad on student visas are not covering these expenses and are often not in contact with the embassy.

Many students arriving for language studies on student visas have been taking up work. However, they are not required to obtain labour permits from the Department of Foreign Employment. As a result, the Foreign Employment Board does not provide financial assistance for repatriation or related support when deaths occur outside the formal labour system.

Deaths and suicides have been reported mainly among workers in construction, Nepal-run hotels and restaurants, and supply companies. Around 6,000 Nepal-operated hotels and restaurants are estimated to be running in Japan, where labour protections such as health insurance and social security are not consistently ensured.

Education consultancies in Nepal have been sending students to Japan by charging high fees and making what critics describe as misleading promises. Japanese government data shows that by 2025, around 116,000 Nepali students were living in Japan, making Nepal the second-largest source of foreign students after China. Overall, Nepalis are the fifth-largest migrant group in Japan, with a total population of about 309,000, including 9,908 permanent residents.

According to the Non-Resident Nepali Association Japan, many students are under severe financial and psychological pressure due to high-interest loans taken in Nepal.

“Living costs in Japan are high, and earnings from 28 working hours a week are not enough for rent, food and tuition,” said NRNA Japan secretary Sachin Acharya. “When families in Nepal demand loan repayments, it adds mental stress. Switching from student visas to work visas requires language proficiency and other conditions, which are difficult. This is contributing to rising suicides.”

He said many students come on student visas due to easier access, but struggle to find stable work. “Some have to rely on money from Nepal. Many Nepalis are being arrested for exceeding the 28-hour work limit,” he said. “The Nepali embassy is understaffed, which makes it difficult to handle prison visits and related cases.”

Nepali student Uma Khatri, currently in Japan, said the reality is far more difficult than expected. “You need strong Japanese language skills before coming here. It is manageable for those who can work hard, but very difficult for students,” she said. “City living is expensive. Rural areas are cheaper, but jobs are scarce. Attendance requirements are strict, and visa renewal can be affected.”

Hira Shrestha from Baglung, who paid Rs1.35 million to reach Japan, said even working beyond permitted hours does not ease financial pressure. “People expect to repay loans quickly, but many struggle for years,” he said. Survival itself is hard.”

He said consultancy firms often present an overly optimistic picture. “They say you can study language for a year and work, but there is no job guarantee. Competition for part-time work is intense,” he said. “Some take multiple jobs to save money, which is illegal and can lead to visa cancellation.”

Only a small number of Nepalis go to Japan as skilled workers, while many enter as trainees in the agriculture and business sectors. The Nepali embassy has urged authorities to avoid sending workers under individual labour permits through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and labour channels.

In the last fiscal year, 18,744 Nepalis received labour approval from the Department of Foreign Employment, including both institutional and individual permits, with 5,800 women among them.

The embassy said it mainly tracks trainee workers sent through approved channels, where employers or agencies can be held responsible in case of death, making repatriation easier. However, it lacks records of students and individuals who arrive outside formal labour approval systems, complicating assistance and monitoring.

articles.title: Nepali workers among injured in Qatar gas plant explosion, 13 killed
articles.summary:
Nepali workers were among those injured in an explosion and fire at a gas processing facility in Qatar, authorities said, as officials confirmed that 13 people were killed and 66 were injured in one of the country’s deadliest industrial accidents in recent years.

The blast occurred on Sunday night at the Barzan gas processing facility inside the Ras Laffan Industrial City complex, according to Qatar Energy officials. The injured include workers from Nepal, Qatar, India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Kenya, Ghana, Tanzania and Nigeria. Authorities said none of the injured is in a critical condition.

Energy minister and president and CEO of QatarEnergy, Saad bin Sherida al-Kaabi, said in Doha that the incident was a “technical accident” and not linked to sabotage or hostile activity. He said emergency teams and civil defence units brought the fire under control quickly.

Al-Kaabi said production at the Barzan facility had been halted for maintenance since December 2025 and was restarted only two days before the incident. He added that Qatar’s liquefied natural gas operations, export systems and port facilities were not affected.

The people killed were Indian and Pakistani nationals, he said.

Al-Kaabi said Qatar has sufficient gas reserves and alternative supply capacity, and the country’s export commitments will not be affected. He also expressed condolences to the families of the deceased and wished the injured a speedy recovery.

Authorities have launched an investigation into the cause of the explosion, Reuters reported.

Al-Kaabi said the incident is under review, while reiterating that there is no impact on wider energy infrastructure.

Qatar hosts one of the world’s largest liquefied natural gas export hubs at Ras Laffan.

articles.title: बालेन्द्र सरकार पाँच वर्ष टिक्नेमा कुलमानको शंका, भन्छन्- चुनावपछि देशको नेतृत्व उज्यालो नेपाल पार्टीले गर्नेछ
articles.summary:
उज्यालो नेपाल पार्टीका अध्यक्ष कुलमान घिसिङले आगामी निर्वाचनपछि बागमती प्रदेशमा आफ्नो पार्टीको नेतृत्वमा सरकार बन्ने दाबी गरेका छन्।

शनिबार काठमाडौंमा आयोजित पार्टी प्रवेश कार्यक्रमलाई सम्बोधन गर्दै उनले बागमती प्रदेशमा मात्र सीमित नरहेर देशव्यापी रूपमा नै उज्यालो नेपाल पार्टीको सरकार बन्ने परिदृश्य तयार भइरहेको बताएका हुन्।

देशमा छिट्टै स्थानीय निकाय र प्रदेशको निर्वाचन हुन गइरहेको उल्लेख गर्दै घिसिङले उक्त चुनावहरूमा उज्यालो नेपाल पार्टीले अत्यधिक सशक्त र प्रभावकारी भूमिका खेल्ने स्पष्ट पारे। उनले भने, ‘आगामी चुनाव, स्थानीय निकायको चुनाव र प्रदेशको चुनाव चाँडै नै आउँदैछ। यसमा उज्यालो नेपाल पार्टीको सशक्त भूमिका रहनेछ र त्यसपछिको चुनावमा उज्यालो नेपाल पार्टीले यो देशको नेतृत्व गर्नेछ।’

अध्यक्ष घिसिङले बालेन्द्र शाह (बालेन) को नेतृत्वमा रहेको राष्ट्रिय स्वतन्त्र पार्टी (रास्वपा) को सरकार दाबी गरिएझैँ पाँच वर्ष टिक्ने सम्भावना नरहेको जिकिर समेत गरे। पछिल्लो चार-पाँच महिनाको काम गराइबाटै वर्तमान सरकारको भविष्य स्पष्ट भइसकेको उनको भनाइ थियो। उनले भने, ‘अहिले तपाईंले जतिसुकै देखे पनि पाँच वर्षको सरकार, पाँच वर्षको सरकार भनेको छ, यो पाँच वर्ष सरकार टिक्ने अवस्थामा पाँच महिनामै देखिसकेको छ, त चार महिनामै देखिसकेको छ। हामीले पाँच वर्ष पनि कुरिरहनुपर्छ जस्तो मलाई लाग्दैन।’

उज्यालो नेपाल पार्टी अब मुलुकको एक मात्र सशक्त र भरपर्दो राजनीतिक विकल्पको रूपमा द्रुत गतिमा स्थापित हुँदै अगाडि बढिरहेको उनको दाबी छ। उज्यालो नेपाल पार्टीलाई हराएर आम जनताले गलत गरेको महसुस गरिसकेको उनले बताए। उनले भने, ‘अहिले तपाईं हरेक गाउँ, गाउँमा, घर-घरमा जानुस्, उज्यालो नेपाल पार्टी र यो पार्टीको नेतृत्व पंक्तिप्रति विश्वास, तपाईंहरू जित्नुपर्थ्यो, हामीले गल्ती गर्‍यौ भन्ने कुरा महसुस भइसकेको छ।’

पुराना तथा स्थापित दलहरूको नेतृत्वप्रति जनताको विश्वास पूर्ण रूपमा टुटिसकेको दाबी गर्दै उनले अब पुराना नेतृत्वका कुनै पनि आश्वासन र कुराहरूमा जनताले विश्वास नगर्ने स्पष्ट पारेका छन्। सो अवसरमा घिसिङले पुराना राजनीतिक दलहरूभित्र रहेका इमानदार र सक्षम नेता-कार्यकर्तालाई उज्यालो नेपाल पार्टीमा प्रवेश गर्न खुला आह्वान समेत गरे।

articles.title: राजतन्त्र पुनबर्हालीको माग गर्दै हस्ताक्षर संकलन अभियान

नेपाललाई अब एक जना स्थाथी अभिभावकको खाँचो रहेको र त्यसका लागि राजा बाहेक अरु विकल्प नै नभएको समूहले जनाएको छ।

सो अभियानमा प्रसिद्ध अभिनेत्री मनिषा कोइरालाले पनि हस्ताक्षर गरेकी छन्। कोइरालाले विभिन्न कार्यक्रममा यसअघि पनि राजाबिना देश नरहने अभिव्यतिहरू दिने गरेकी छन्।

articles.title: छिट्टै ‘ऐतिहासिक सम्झौता’ हुने भन्दै ट्रम्पले इरानमाथिको आक्रमण रोके
articles.summary:
अमेरिकी राष्ट्रपति डोनाल्ड ट्रम्पले इरानसँग 'छिट्टै सम्झौता गर्न सक्षम हुने' सर्तमा आफूले इरानविरुद्ध तय गरेको सैन्य आक्रमण रद्द गरेको घोषणा गरेका छन्।

ट्रुथ सोसलमा एक पोस्ट गर्दै उनले इरान र मध्य पूर्वका अन्य देशहरूले सम्झौताको मापदण्डमा सहमति भइसकेको भन्दै आक्रमण रोक्न अनुरोध गरेपछि यो निर्णय लिइएको प्रस्ट पारेका हुन्। ट्रम्पका अनुसार नयाँ बन्ने सम्झौतामा रणनीतिक रूपमा महत्त्वपूर्ण मानिने होर्मुज जलमार्गको तत्काल र पूर्ण खुलासहित इरानको आणविक खतराको सधैंका लागि अन्त्य गर्ने विषय समावेश छ।

उनले विश्वको भविष्यको हित र सफल तथा समृद्ध इरानको अस्तित्वका लागि आक्रमण स्थगन गर्न सहमत भएको बताए। साथै, इजरायल पनि इरानसँगको सम्झौताको यो मार्गमा अमेरिकासँग सहकार्य गर्न सहमत भएको उनको भनाइ छ। तर अमेरिका जुनसुकै परिस्थितिमा पनि कडा रूपमा प्रस्तुत हुन तयार रहेको उनको चेतावनी छ।

यसैबिच, इरानी विदेशमन्त्री अब्बास अराघाचीले टर्की, पाकिस्तान र साउदी अरेबियाका विदेशमन्त्रीहरूसँग छुट्टाछुट्टै टेलिफोन वार्ता गर्दै अमेरिका र इजरायलको तर्फबाट हुने जुनसुकै ‘आक्रमण’ को कडा र ‘टिट फर ट्याट’ जवाफ दिने चेतावनी दिएका थिए।

अमेरिका र इजरायलले इरानको ऊर्जा पूर्वाधारलाई लक्षित गरी अहिलेसम्मकै कठोर नयाँ आक्रमणको तयारी गरिरहेको भन्ने रिपोर्टहरू बाहिरिएलगत्तै इरानले यस्तो कडा प्रतिक्रिया दिएको थियो।

यसअघि, साउदी अरेबियाका युवराज मोहम्मद बिन सलमानले ट्रम्पसँग फोन संवाद गर्दै अमेरिकाले इरानसँगको द्वन्द्व थप बढाएमा त्यसले सम्पूर्ण खाडी क्षेत्रको ऊर्जा र अन्य प्रमुख पूर्वाधारमा गम्भीर असर पार्न सक्ने भन्दै गहिरो चिन्ता व्यक्त गरेका थिए।

साउदी पक्षले द्वन्द्व थप नचर्कियोस् भनेर अमेरिका र इरानलाई वार्ताको टेबलमा फर्कन निरन्तर आग्रह गर्दै आएको छ। यस हप्ताको सुरुमा साउदी अरेबियाले इराकमा इरानी-समर्थित मिलिसियाहरूविरुद्धका कारबाहीमा अमेरिकासँग सहयोग गरे पनि समग्र क्षेत्रमा शान्ति कायम होस् भन्ने पक्षमा देखिएको छ।

गत फेब्रुअरीको अन्त्यबाट अमेरिका र इजरायलले इरानविरुद्ध सैन्य कारबाही सुरु गरेयता दुवै पक्षबिच हमला र प्रति-हमलाहरू बढ्दै गएका छन्। हालै जोर्डनस्थित अमेरिकी अखडामा इरानले गरेको आक्रमणलाई अमेरिकी सेनाले विफल पारेपछि राष्ट्रपति ट्रम्पले बदला लिने वाचा गरेका थिए।

ह्वाइट हाउसकी प्रेस सचिव क्यारोलिन लेभिटले तेहरानले गत महिनाको युद्धविराम समझदारी तोडेको, व्यावसायिक जहाजहरूमा गोली हानेको र अमेरिकी सैनिकहरूलाई मारेको भन्दै रोष प्रकट गरेकी थिइन्।

मध्य पूर्वमा बढ्दो तनाव, सम्भावित उडान रद्द र हवाई क्षेत्र बन्द हुन सक्ने जोखिमलाई मध्यनजर गर्दै अमेरिकी विदेश विभागले यस क्षेत्रमा रहेका अमेरिकी नागरिकहरूलाई उच्च सतर्कता अपनाउन र सुरक्षा सावधानी बढाउन नयाँ सुरक्षा सतर्कता जारी गरेको छ।

द्वन्द्वका कारण विश्व अर्थतन्त्र प्रभावित बन्दै गएको छ, जसले मध्यावधि निर्वाचनको संघारमा रहेका ट्रम्पमाथि पनि दबाब बढाएको छ।
